definition: A building constructed to one tenant's specifications, under a lease signed before it is finished.
The date you promised to hand a finished hall over to the tenant, ready for service.
The last possible date to deliver before the tenant can walk away from that hall.
A pre-agreed daily cash penalty you owe the tenant for every day a hall is late.
Free rent months owed to the tenant later, instead of a cash penalty, to make up for a late hall.
A lease where the tenant pays taxes, insurance, and upkeep on top of rent.
A scheduled yearly bump in rent, agreed in the lease ahead of time.
The regulator's official case file for a request, like your power agreement, that needs a public vote.
A group that formally joins a docket to argue for or against what you are asking for.
A formal request for documents or answers from you during a regulatory case.
Written or spoken evidence you file to support your case before a vote.
The utility's engineering review of how your campus will connect to and affect the grid.
A large piece of electrical equipment that steps power up or down; it can take years to build and ship.
Equipment that switches and protects electrical circuits; another long-lead item you have to order early.
The site facility that steps down grid power to a voltage your halls can use.
A fee you pay the utility for power capacity you reserved but are not yet using.
Power usage effectiveness: total site power divided by power that reaches the computers. Lower is more efficient.
The power actually used by computing equipment, not counting cooling or site overhead.
The amount of power your campus is actually pulling from the utility's grid.
Megawatt: a unit of power. One megawatt can run roughly a thousand homes.
A unit of rent: dollars charged per kilowatt of capacity, per month.
The first-priority construction loan; it gets paid back before any other debt or equity.
A second loan layered between the senior loan and equity, riskier and more expensive than senior debt.
Paid-in-kind interest: interest that adds to the loan balance instead of being paid in cash.
The ownership money in the deal; it is paid back last and takes the most risk.
The full mix of senior debt, mezzanine debt, and equity that funds a project.
Loan-to-cost: the share of total project cost a loan will fund.
A request to pull funds from a committed loan or equity source to pay that month's bills.
Loan interest added to the loan balance during construction instead of paid in cash.
A rule in a loan agreement that you must keep meeting or risk default.
Debt service coverage ratio: income divided by debt payments owed. More headroom above the covenant trigger means more cushion before default.
The test a construction loan must pass to convert to cheaper, permanent financing.
A higher interest rate charged after a loan fails its conversion test.
Refinancing the construction loan with permanent debt once the project is stable.
Capitalization rate: a property's yearly income divided by its value. Lower cap rate means higher value.
Net operating income: rent collected minus the landlord's operating costs.
What you get back divided by what you put in, in equity.
Insurance that covers physical damage to a project while it is under construction.
Insurance that covers lost income and extra costs caused by an insured construction delay.
The amount you pay out of pocket on an insurance claim before coverage kicks in.
Guaranteed maximum price: a contract where the builder absorbs cost overruns past an agreed cap.
A contract where you pay the builder's actual costs plus a fee, overruns included.
The official sign-off that a building is safe and legal to use.
Cooling computer racks with liquid instead of air; needed for the densest chips.
A standardized frame holding rows of computing equipment.
A company that runs cloud or AI computing at a massive, global scale.
The reduced value assigned to a hall that is unfinished or sitting empty at sale time.
A firm that grades how likely a loan or bond is to be repaid.
The closing table: where the money comes from (senior loan, mezzanine, equity) and what it pays for (land, halls, power gear, working capital). The two sides must balance.
How the loan and equity actually fund over time: each month of construction calls equity first, then mezzanine, then the senior loan, and only then your cash.
Before conversion, loan interest is added to the loan balance (capitalized) instead of paid in cash - the loan effectively funds its own interest while you build.
The order money leaves the project each month: burn, insurance, utility minimums and damages come out of cash, while construction is funded down the equity-mezz-senior stack first.
The next twelve months of rent income, net of the landlord's cost share, from halls already delivered. Lenders divide it by annual debt payments to get your DSCR.
The project sponsor: finds the site, wins the permits, signs the lease, raises the money and holds every risk nobody else agreed to take. In this game, that is you.
The firm that runs the site: crews, schedule, subcontractors, inspections. A GMP contract moves cost overruns above the cap to the GC.
The power company: studies your grid connection, builds the plants and sets the minimum monthly charge. A higher minimum charge moves some plant-slip risk to it.
The bank behind the senior loan. It releases money draw by draw, can freeze draws when progress looks wrong, and tests your DSCR covenant at conversion.
Carries what it prices: builder's risk for physical damage, DSU for lost rent after an insured delay. Anything you declined to cover stays with you.
The utility's ordinary customers. Plants built for a campus that never uses them usually end up in everyone's rates - which is why their advocates intervene in your docket.
The investor supplying most of the committed equity. Its share decides how much of the final equity value is yours.
The regulator that votes on the docket letting the utility build for your load. Testimony, discovery and intervenor settlements move the vote.
Money held back on top of your cost call for surprises. A bigger cushion makes the loan larger and costs a bigger lender fee.
The lender checks that the money left to draw covers what is left to build. If it does not, the loan is out of balance and draws stop.
You ask your partner to put in more cash. It fixes a shortfall, but your share dilutes and the new money counts against your equity multiple.
A short, expensive loan from you or a sponsor. It pays interest in kind at about 14% and is repaid ahead of equity when you take out the project.
Cancel a hall you have not finished. You pay a termination fee and lose what you spent, and get some salvage back. The tenant will notice.
A mid-construction refinance. The lender raises the loan for a fee and a higher rate, so you get cash now and a bigger bill at takeout.
When new equity comes in at a premium, your slice of the project shrinks by more than the cash raised.
Months to clear and prepare the ground before vertical construction can start on a hall.
